questions.q: An angle measures 72°. A pupil writes 108°. What went wrong?
questions.model: 72 + 108 = 180: the two scales always add up to 180°. The angle is acute, so 72° is correct; 108° came from the other scale.

questions.q: Draw an angle of 140°. Which type is it?
To draw 300°, what angle do you draw first?
Measure the six angles a to f on the printable angle sheet, then draw angles of 40°, 125° and 250°.
questions.a: Sheet: a 35°, b 118°, c 90°, d 162°, e 205°, f 330° (accept ± 2°). 250° is drawn as 110° inside with the outside marked.
questions.model: Angle a: centre on the vertex, zero line on the lower arm, read the inner scale from 0: 35°. It looks acute, so 35° (not 145°) is sensible.

questions.q: Without measuring, explain why angles of 175° and 185° look almost the same.
questions.a: Both are 5° from a straight line (180°), one on each side.

questions.q: Draw triangle ABC with AB = 8 cm, angle A = 50° and angle B = 60°. Measure angle C. What should it be?
questions.a: 70°, because the angles in a triangle add up to 180°

questions.q: The inside angle is 100°. The reflex angle is:
Where does the centre cross of the protractor go?
questions.a: On the vertex of the angle

questions.q: Big question: why do the two scales cause wrong answers, and how do you avoid it?
questions.a: Each angle can be read as x or 180 - x; start from 0 on your arm and decide acute or obtuse first.
